By December we will have broken even.
So, twelve months out. Where is the transport arm going to be?
It broke even in month fourteen, which was ahead of the plan. By December we will have doubled the fleet.
Doubled from what, and is that decided or expected?
Decided. We are signing for the vehicles in January, and we are phasing them in across the first quarter rather than all at once.
And the second line at plant two?
That one is expected rather than arranged. We are going to bring it forward to August if the volume holds, and there is a window for the capital expenditure in the first quarter or not at all.
What does the year look like if the volume does not hold?
Then this time next year we will be running one line with more headroom than I would like, and I would rather tell you that now than in June.

We built the plan in October and by February about a third of it was already wrong, which I have stopped treating as a failure. The parts that survived were the parts with a date and a name against them. We were signing for the vehicles in January, that happened. We were kicking the pilot off on the ninth of March, that happened too. What did not survive was everything phrased as we will look at, or we will consider, because a sentence like that has nobody in it and no day in it, so it quietly becomes next quarter and then next year. This time next year we will be running the second line, and I say that with a straight face because the capital is approved and the window is booked. Whereas if you had asked me in October I would have said we are going to expand, which sounded confident and meant almost nothing. The test I use now is simple. If the sentence has no date, it is not a plan, it is a hope with good grammar.

People come to me expecting to be told their forecast was too optimistic, and quite often it was not. The number was reasonable when it was built. What went wrong is that nothing was set up to notice when the assumption underneath it stopped being true. A forecast is a sentence about the world on the day you wrote it, and it starts ageing immediately. So the question I ask is not how confident are you, it is what would have to happen for this to be wrong, and when would you find out. If the answer to the second one is in December, then the forecast is not a forecast, it is a report you will read too late. The companies that handle this well do something unglamorous. They write down two or three things that would tell them early, they put a date on checking them, and they name a person. By March they either know they are on track or they know they are not, and either of those is worth more than a better number in October.

If you look at automation projects in mid-sized manufacturing, the pattern in the data is almost boringly consistent. The equipment arrives roughly when it was supposed to. The line is running roughly when it was supposed to be running. And then the project takes another year and a half, because the part nobody scheduled was the part where people learn to work differently around it. Firms that phase it in, one line or one plant at a time, report longer plans and shorter overruns, which sounds like a contradiction until you see what the phased approach actually buys: by the time the second plant starts, everybody knows what went wrong at the first one. The ones that do it everywhere at once are usually responding to a window, a capital approval or a client deadline, and they will tell you afterwards that they would take the slower route if they were doing it again. What none of them say is that the technology failed. It almost never does.
